title: Problem Overview: Asymptotic Formula for ex(n; C4)
content: Erdos Problem #765 asks for the growth rate of ex(n; C4), the maximum number of edges in an n-vertex graph with no 4-cycle. Answer: ex(n; C4) ~ (1/2)n^{3/2}. Solved through contributions spanning 45 years: Erdos-Klein (1938) established the order, Reiman (1958) refined the constants, Erdos-Renyi-Brown provided the construction, and Furedi (1983) proved exact values. Erdos's refined conjecture about lower-order terms was disproved by Ma-Yang (2023).
mathContext: $\text{ex}(n; C_4) \sim \frac{1}{2} n^{3/2}$, meaning $\lim_{n \to \infty} \text{ex}(n; C_4) / n^{3/2} = 1/2$. For $n = q^2 + q + 1$ with $q$ prime power $> 13$: $\text{ex}(n; C_4) = \frac{1}{2}q(q+1)^2$ exactly (Furedi). Erdos's conjecture $\text{ex}(n; C_4) = \frac{1}{2}n^{3/2} + \frac{1}{4}n + O(\sqrt{n})$ was DISPROVED (Ma-Yang 2023).

title: 4-Cycle, C4-Free, and Edge Count Definitions
content: hasFourCycle G requires 4 distinct vertices v1, v2, v3, v4 with all 6 distinctness conditions and 4 adjacency edges forming a cycle. isFourCycleFree G negates hasFourCycle. Equivalently, no two vertices share more than one common neighbor (the 'no repeated paths' characterization). edgeCount uses G.edgeFinset.card for the number of edges.
mathContext: `hasFourCycle(G) := \exists v_1, v_2, v_3, v_4$ pairwise distinct with $G.\text{Adj}(v_i, v_{i+1 \mod 4})$. `isFourCycleFree(G) := \neg\text{hasFourCycle}(G)$. Equivalently: $\forall u, v, |N(u) \cap N(v)| \leq 1$. `edgeCount(G) = G.\text{edgeFinset.card}$.

title: Extremal Function ex(n; C4)
content: ex_C4 n (axiom) is the maximum number of edges in an n-vertex C4-free graph. ex_C4_realized guarantees existence of an optimal C4-free graph achieving this count. The extremal function is the central object: understanding its asymptotics answers Problem #765.
mathContext: `ex_C4(n) := \max\{|E(G)| : |V(G)| = n, G \text{ is } C_4\text{-free}\}$. `ex_C4_realized(n)` ensures $\exists G$ with $|V| = n$, $\text{isFourCycleFree}(G)$, and $|E(G)| = \text{ex\_C4}(n)$. This is the Zarankiewicz number $z(n; 2)$.

title: Historical Bounds: Erdos-Klein, Reiman, Projective Planes
content: Three key axiomatized bounds. erdos_klein_upper (1938): ex(n;C4) <= c * n^{3/2} for some c > 0, proved via double counting of 2-paths (each pair of vertices shares at most one common neighbor). reiman_bounds (1958): the limit L = lim ex(n;C4)/n^{3/2} satisfies 1/(2*sqrt(2)) <= L <= 1/2. projective_plane_construction: for n = q^2+q+1 with q prime power, ex(n;C4) >= (1/2)q(q+1)^2 via the incidence graph of PG(2,q).
mathContext: `erdos_klein_upper : \exists c > 0, \text{ex\_C4}(n) \leq c \cdot n^{3/2}$. Proof: double count 2-paths; $C_4$-free means $\leq 1$ common neighbor per pair, so $\sum \binom{\deg(v)}{2} \leq \binom{n}{2}$, giving $|E| \leq \frac{1}{2}(1 + \sqrt{2n-1})n/2$. `reiman_bounds : 1/(2\sqrt{2}) \leq L \leq 1/2$. `projective_plane_construction : \text{ex\_C4}(q^2+q+1) \geq \frac{1}{2}q(q+1)^2$.

title: Main Theorem: ex(n; C4) ~ (1/2)n^{3/2}
content: asymptotic_ratio n = ex_C4(n)/n^{3/2} (with 0 for n=0). asymptotic_formula (axiom): for all epsilon > 0, exists N such that |asymptotic_ratio(n) - 1/2| < epsilon for n >= N. erdos_765 (PROVED): the main theorem, proved by direct application of asymptotic_formula. This combines the Erdos-Klein upper bound (lim sup <= 1/2) with the projective plane lower bound (lim inf >= 1/2).
mathContext: $r(n) = \text{ex\_C4}(n)/n^{3/2}$. `asymptotic_formula : \forall \varepsilon > 0, \exists N, \forall n \geq N, |r(n) - 1/2| < \varepsilon$. `erdos_765 := asymptotic_formula`. The limit follows from: upper bound $\limsup r(n) \leq 1/2$ (Erdos-Klein/Reiman) and lower bound $\liminf r(n) \geq 1/2$ (projective planes at $n = q^2+q+1$).

title: Furedi's Exact Result (1983)
content: furedi_exact (axiom): for q > 13 prime power and n = q^2+q+1, ex(n;C4) = (1/2)q(q+1)^2 exactly. The projective plane incidence graph PG(2,q) is the unique extremal graph (up to isomorphism) for these parameters. This gives exact values for infinitely many n, not just asymptotic bounds.
mathContext: `furedi_exact : q > 13 \Rightarrow \text{ex\_C4}(q^2+q+1) = q(q+1)^2/2$. The incidence graph of $PG(2,q)$ has $q^2+q+1$ vertices (points), $q^2+q+1$ vertices (lines), and $q+1$ edges per vertex, totaling $(q^2+q+1)(q+1)/2$ edges. The $C_4$-free property follows from: two points determine a unique line in a projective plane.

title: Erdos's Conjecture and Ma-Yang Disproof (2023)
content: erdos_refined_upper (axiom): ex(n;C4) <= (1/2)n^{3/2} + (1/4)n + c*sqrt(n) for some c. erdos_conjecture (definition): the lower bound also holds with coefficient 1/4. ma_yang_disproof (axiom): there exists c > 0 and delta > 0 such that for all N, a positive-density subset S of [1,N] satisfies ex(n;C4) <= (1/2)n^{3/2} + (1/4 - c)*n for all n in S. This means the coefficient 1/4 is NOT tight.
mathContext: `erdos_refined_upper : \text{ex\_C4}(n) \leq \frac{1}{2}n^{3/2} + \frac{1}{4}n + O(\sqrt{n})$. `erdos_conjecture := \exists c, \forall n, |\text{ex\_C4}(n) - (\frac{1}{2}n^{3/2} + \frac{1}{4}n)| \leq c\sqrt{n}$. `ma_yang_disproof : \exists c > 0, \delta > 0, \forall N, \exists S \subseteq [1,N], |S| \geq \delta N \wedge \forall n \in S, \text{ex\_C4}(n) \leq \frac{1}{2}n^{3/2} + (\frac{1}{4}-c)n$.

title: B2 Sequences (Sidon Sets) Connection
content: is_B2_sequence A: all pairwise sums a+b (a <= b, a,b in A) are distinct. Formally: a+b = c+d with a <= b, c <= d implies a = c and b = d. Erdos discovered ex(n;C4) = O(n^{3/2}) in 1936 while studying B2 sequences (Problem #425). A B2 set of size k in [1,n] yields a C4-free bipartite graph, connecting additive combinatorics to extremal graph theory.
mathContext: `is_B2_sequence(A) := \forall a,b,c,d \in A, a \leq b \wedge c \leq d \wedge a+b = c+d \Rightarrow a = c \wedge b = d$. A $B_2$ set of size $k$ in $[1,n]$ gives $\binom{k}{2} \leq n$ distinct sums, so $k = O(\sqrt{n})$. The bipartite incidence graph (elements vs. sums) is $C_4$-free.

title: Projective Plane Examples (4 PROVED)
content: Four projective plane vertex counts proved by simp+ring. fano_plane_example: PG(2,2) has 7 vertices (the Fano plane, smallest projective plane). pg23_example: PG(2,3) has 13 vertices. pg24_example: PG(2,4) has 21 vertices (4 = 2^2 is prime power but not prime). pg25_example: PG(2,5) has 31 vertices. Each uses projectivePlaneVertices q = q^2 + q + 1.
mathContext: `fano_plane_example : 2^2 + 2 + 1 = 7`. `pg23_example : 3^2 + 3 + 1 = 13`. `pg24_example : 4^2 + 4 + 1 = 21`. `pg25_example : 5^2 + 5 + 1 = 31`. All proved by `simp [projectivePlaneVertices]; ring`. The Fano plane has 7 points, 7 lines, 3 points per line, 3 lines per point.
